where: Figure (comparison of box and Gaussian weight)
problem: The two curves are plotted on different, unnormalised scales, so the picture contradicts the numbers in Section 2. The Gaussian series is exp(-x²/2), which is 1 at d = 0 and has no 1/(√(2π)σ) factor, while the text's mask weights are G(d) divided by the sum (centre 0.25, edge 0.125, corner 0.0625). The box is drawn at weight 1, not 1/9 ≈ 0.111. Read literally, the figure says the box weight (1) is larger than the Gaussian weight (0.61) at d = 1, which is the reverse of the real 3 × 3 masks (0.125 Gaussian vs 0.111 box).
fix: Plot normalised mask weights: box flat at 1/9 ≈ 0.111 out to the window edge, Gaussian at 0.25 at the centre falling to 0.125 at one pixel and 0.0625 at the corner for the 1 2 1 / 2 4 2 / 1 2 1 mask, or relabel the axis 'relative weight (each curve scaled to its own maximum)' and say in the caption that only the shape is being compared.

where: Section 3, sentence on repeated smoothing in hardware
problem: The sentence mixes two different ideas. 'Apply the separable 1-D mask twice' describes separability, which is what one single Gaussian pass already needs (once along rows, once along columns). Two Gaussian passes need four 1-D passes, not two. A student will think repeated smoothing and separability are the same saving.
fix: Two small Gaussian passes therefore approximate one larger Gaussian. This is useful in hardware: apply a small 3 × 3 mask twice (four 1-D passes in all, two along rows and two along columns) instead of storing and running one large 2-D mask.

problem: The text says 'the same rule applies at borders' but does not say which sum to divide by. If a student averages only the pixels that exist and then divides by the full mask sum (16 for the 3 × 3 Gaussian), the border darkens — the exact fault the paragraph warns about. Zero padding does the same.
fix: When you average only over pixels that exist, divide by the sum of the weights of those pixels only (for example 9 of the 16 for a corner of the 1 2 1 mask). When you pad, use replicate or mirror padding, not zeros, so the sum stays 16 and no dark border appears.
